name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
meta_description: Investigative consulting for matters touching Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: international company and trust research, asset tracing and ECSC litigation support.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Saint Vincent and the Grenadines often involves international companies, trusts and brokers that appear in cross-border disputes, together with tourism and real estate counterparties. Work focuses on lawful records research, ownership analysis and support for counsel before the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court.
intro: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines has a common law legal system, with magistrates' courts, a family court and the Supreme Court of Judicature, comprising the High Court and the Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal. Final appeals go to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council; the Caribbean Court of Justice has original jurisdiction on CARICOM treaty matters. Domestic business registration is handled on paper by the Commerce and Intellectual Property Office, typically with attorneys preparing incorporation documents. Courts are widely regarded as slow. For investigators, the most important features are a well-used international business and trust regime and limited public access to ownership information.

Organisations commission investigative work involving Saint Vincent and the Grenadines most often because entities formed there appear in international structures, including companies, trusts and online trading or brokerage businesses linked to complaints by investors in other countries. Litigants, insolvency practitioners and compliance teams need to understand who controls such entities and where assets have gone. Other matters concern tourism and real estate development in the Grenadines, renewable energy, agro-processing and ICT projects. Typical exposures include asset dissipation through offshore vehicles, misrepresented regulatory status, undisclosed ownership and counterparties whose public claims cannot be reconciled with records.
legal_system: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines has a common law legal system derived from English law, with judicial independence guaranteed by the Constitution. Lower courts are the magistrates' courts and a family court. The Supreme Court of Judicature, established under the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court Act, comprises the High Court and the Eastern Caribbean Court of Appeal, with final appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The Arbitration Act of 1952 governs arbitration and the enforcement of foreign arbitral awards.

data_protection.law: Privacy Act (2003); no specific comprehensive data protection legislation identified
data_protection.summary: According to the 2024 US State Department assessment, a Privacy Act was passed in 2003 but the government has not adopted specific data protection legislation. There is therefore no identified data protection authority or general cross-border transfer regime. Investigations involving personal data about individuals in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines should still respect constitutional protections, the confidentiality duties of banks, trustees and other regulated service providers, and the common law of confidence. TDSC applies data minimisation, defined purposes, secure storage and controlled retention as standard practice and confirms any local collection with counsel.

investigator_regulation: We have not identified, from official sources available to us, a dedicated licensing regime for private investigators in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. The lawfulness of local investigative steps, including surveillance, recording and approaches to witnesses or service providers, should be confirmed with local counsel in advance. Information held by registered agents, trustees and financial institutions is subject to confidentiality and is generally obtained only through court process or regulatory channels. TDSC therefore concentrates on documentary research and supports counsel in seeking disclosure where it is needed.
corporate_records: Domestic companies are registered with the Commerce and Intellectual Property Office (CIPO), alongside registration with the Inland Revenue Department and the National Insurance Services; registration is paper-based and takes about two business days. International companies and trusts are formed under separate legislation, with trusts recorded by a Registrar of Trusts and at least one licensed trustee required. Non-nationals need a licence to acquire more than 50 percent of a company. We have not confirmed what shareholder or beneficial ownership information is publicly searchable; it is generally not public for international entities. Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court judgments are published.
anti_corruption: Official corruption carries criminal penalties under national law, with the Royal Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Police Force investigating and the Director of Public Prosecutions prosecuting offences. There is generally no statutory duty for public officers to disclose their finances. The Financial Intelligence Unit can conduct financial investigations with a court order, and 2022 virtual asset legislation requires virtual asset businesses to register. Banks are supervised by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank and securities by the Eastern Caribbean Securities Regulatory Commission.

matters.title: Online broker and trading complaints
matters.text: Research into online trading, forex and brokerage businesses that cite incorporation in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, comparing their claims about regulation and ownership with available records, litigation and regulatory warnings elsewhere, to support counsel acting for investors or payment providers.

matters.title: International trust and company tracing
matters.text: Mapping international companies and trusts formed in the jurisdiction within wider asset structures, using litigation records, foreign filings and client documents, and supporting counsel seeking disclosure orders against registered agents or trustees through the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court.

matters.title: Grenadines real estate diligence
matters.text: Background research on developers, sellers and project sponsors in the Grenadines and on mainland Saint Vincent, covering corporate history, land holding licences for non-nationals, prior projects, disputes and media, for purchasers, lenders and investors.

matters.title: Judgment and award enforcement support
matters.text: Lawful research into assets and corporate interests of debtors connected with the jurisdiction, to support enforcement of foreign judgments and arbitral awards, coordinated with local counsel given the pace of local proceedings.

matters.title: Infrastructure and energy counterparties
matters.text: Verifying the ownership, track record and integrity history of contractors and partners in renewable energy, port, airport and tourism infrastructure projects, including checks for related parties and adverse media in the region and beyond.

tdsc_approach: TDSC scopes engagements touching Saint Vincent and the Grenadines from Nashville and first distinguishes domestic companies from international companies and trusts, because the governing legislation, records and confidentiality rules differ. Research draws on registry information available through lawful channels, published Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court and Privy Council judgments, regulatory warnings in other jurisdictions, foreign filings and media. Where ownership or asset information is held by registered agents, trustees or banks, TDSC works with counsel on court-based disclosure rather than informal approaches. Personal data is minimised and securely handled even though no comprehensive data protection statute has been identified. Local steps are rare, agreed with counsel and carried out by qualified professionals. TDSC does not provide legal advice.

faqs.q: A broker says it is registered in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. What does that mean?
faqs.a: Incorporation in the jurisdiction does not by itself indicate that a business is licensed to provide investment services. TDSC compares a firm's claims with available registry information, regulatory warnings in other countries, litigation and media, and reports discrepancies so counsel can decide on next steps.

faqs.q: Can you identify the beneficiaries of a trust formed in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines?
faqs.a: Not from public records. Trust information is held by licensed trustees and the Registrar of Trusts and is confidential. We gather circumstantial evidence from litigation, transactions and related entities, and support counsel who may seek disclosure through the court where the legal grounds exist.

faqs.q: Is there a data protection law in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines?
faqs.a: A Privacy Act was passed in 2003, but as of 2024 the US State Department reported that no specific data protection legislation had been adopted. TDSC nonetheless applies its own minimisation, security and retention standards and respects banking and trust confidentiality obligations.

faqs.q: How long do court proceedings take there?
faqs.a: The court system is widely regarded as slow, and enforcement can take time. For clients pursuing assets or enforcing judgments, early and accurate research on the debtor's structures helps counsel decide whether local proceedings, action in other jurisdictions or settlement offers the best route.

faqs.q: Can non-nationals freely buy property or companies there?
faqs.a: Not without approval in some cases. Non-nationals need a licence to acquire more than 50 percent of a company, and companies holding larger landholdings may restrict share transfers to non-Vincentians. Property diligence therefore checks whether required approvals exist, alongside the seller's and developer's history.
